questions.prompt: You run GRANT SELECT ON SCHEMA main.analytics TO GROUP data_analysts. A colleague creates a new Delta table main.analytics.q4_results the following day. Members of data_analysts query the new table. What happens?

options.label: Query fails — GRANT SELECT ON SCHEMA covers only objects existing at grant time; new tables require an additional explicit grant
Query succeeds — GRANT ON SCHEMA automatically cascades to all current and future child objects
Query succeeds only if the table creator also belongs to data_analysts
Query fails because analysts need GRANT SELECT ON CATALOG, not on the schema level

questions.explanation: In Unity Catalog, GRANT SELECT ON SCHEMA grants access to objects that existed at grant time. New tables created after the grant are not automatically covered. Administrators must issue an additional grant or configure default privileges for future objects.

questions.prompt: Your team runs hourly ETL pipelines that each take 8 minutes to complete. A senior engineer proposes keeping one all-purpose cluster running 24/7 to eliminate the 4-minute job-cluster startup time. What is the primary cost argument against this approach?

options.label: All-purpose clusters cannot execute scheduled Databricks Jobs — only interactive notebook sessions are supported
The cluster accrues 52 minutes of idle DBU billing per hour to avoid 4 minutes of startup; job clusters start on demand and terminate immediately after each run
Continuous clusters are restricted to a single concurrent Spark job, serializing the hourly pipeline runs
All-purpose clusters reset Spark session state between tasks, causing non-deterministic behavior in scheduled pipelines

questions.explanation: All-purpose clusters accrue DBU costs every minute they run. A 24/7 cluster running 8-minute hourly jobs spends ~88% of its time idle. Job clusters avoid this cost profile by starting fresh per run and terminating immediately upon completion.

questions.prompt: A service principal is granted SELECT on table prod.finance.invoices but has no other Unity Catalog grants. It runs SELECT * FROM prod.finance.invoices and receives a SCHEMA_NOT_FOUND error. What is the most likely missing privilege?

options.label: CREATE TABLE on prod.finance — required even for read-only access to managed Delta tables
MODIFY on prod.finance.invoices — SELECT alone does not allow row-level data access in Unity Catalog
USE CATALOG on prod and USE SCHEMA on prod.finance — without these the three-level namespace cannot be traversed to reach the table
GRANT SELECT must be re-approved by a workspace admin after each cluster restart before it takes effect

questions.explanation: Unity Catalog requires USE CATALOG and USE SCHEMA in addition to SELECT on the target table. Without the traversal privileges the SQL engine cannot resolve the fully qualified name even when SELECT is granted, raising a namespace-not-found error.

questions.prompt: A data engineer retrieves a database connection string from a Databricks secret scope and passes it to a Python logging function that writes to the cluster driver log. What does Databricks do with the secret value in that log output?

options.label: Logs the full plaintext value — Databricks only redacts secrets in notebook cell output, not in driver logs
Raises a PermissionError before the secret is passed to the logging function
Encrypts the value in-place with a workspace key before appending it to the log file
Replaces the secret value with [REDACTED] in driver logs, cluster event history, and notebook cell output

questions.explanation: Databricks Secret Scopes redact secret values wherever they appear in Databricks-managed output — notebook cells, driver logs, and cluster event history — replacing them with [REDACTED]. This prevents accidental credential exposure regardless of how the secret is used in code.

questions.prompt: You are a data engineer at CityMoves Transit. You provision a cluster for the workspace exploration lab. The cluster is idle for 40 minutes with no active Spark jobs or notebook connections. What happens?

codeSnippet.code:
cluster_config = {
    "cluster_name": "citymoves-analytics",
    "spark_version": "14.3.x-scala2.12",
    "node_type_id": "Standard_DS3_v2",
    "autoscale": {"min_workers": 1, "max_workers": 8},
    "autotermination_minutes": 30
}

options.label: Cluster terminates automatically because it has been idle longer than autotermination_minutes (30)
Cluster scales down to 0 workers but keeps running to preserve the Spark session context
Cluster switches to SQL Warehouse mode after the autotermination window expires
Cluster sends an idle alert to the workspace admin but continues running indefinitely

questions.explanation: autotermination_minutes = 30 means the cluster shuts down automatically after 30 minutes of inactivity. At 40 minutes idle the cluster will have already terminated, freeing compute and stopping DBU accrual.

codeSnippet.code:
db_password = dbutils.secrets.get(
    scope="patient-records-scope",
    key="postgres-password"
)
print(db_password)

options.label: The full plaintext password — Databricks decrypts secrets for the calling notebook and print() outputs the result
[REDACTED] — Databricks masks secret values in all notebook outputs and driver logs
A Python PermissionError because print() is blocked for secret-backed variables in secure workspaces
An empty string because the key has not yet been populated in the scope

questions.explanation: Databricks Secret Scopes redact resolved values wherever they appear in Databricks-managed output, replacing them with [REDACTED]. This prevents accidental credential exposure in cell output, driver logs, and notebook revision history regardless of how the secret is used in code.

questions.prompt: You are a data engineer at CityMoves Transit. Your team registered public transit data in Unity Catalog. What three-level namespace does this query use?

codeSnippet.code:
SELECT route_id, stop_name, daily_ridership
FROM citymoves_prod.transit_ops.daily_ridership
WHERE trip_date = '2024-03-15'
ORDER BY daily_ridership DESC;

options.label: workspace.database.table — the legacy Hive metastore format used before Unity Catalog
metastore.catalog.object — used for cross-workspace federation queries only
catalog.schema.table — the Unity Catalog three-level namespace: citymoves_prod → transit_ops → daily_ridership
environment.domain.object — used exclusively for external tables backed by cloud storage

questions.explanation: Unity Catalog organizes all data assets in a three-level hierarchy: catalog.schema.object. Here citymoves_prod is the catalog, transit_ops is the schema, and daily_ridership is the table.

questions.prompt: You are building a parameterized deployment notebook for a patient records platform. A Databricks Job task runs this notebook with target_env = 'prod'. What does dbutils.notebook.exit() do in this context?

codeSnippet.code:
env = dbutils.widgets.get("target_env")
catalog = f"{env}_catalog"
schema = f"{env}_patient_data"
spark.sql(f"USE CATALOG {catalog}")
spark.sql(f"USE SCHEMA {schema}")
dbutils.notebook.exit(f"Targeting: {catalog}.{schema}")

options.label: Terminates the Databricks cluster that the notebook is running on
Commits all pending Spark transactions and closes open Delta table writers
Deletes the target_env widget from the current session to prevent reuse in subsequent runs
Returns the string 'Targeting: prod_catalog.prod_patient_data' to the calling Job task so downstream tasks can read it via dbutils.jobs.taskValues

questions.explanation: dbutils.notebook.exit() exits the notebook and returns a string value to the calling context — either a parent notebook that used dbutils.notebook.run() or a Databricks Job task. The calling Job task can then access this exit value through task values for downstream orchestration decisions.

questions.prompt: You are a data engineer at CityMoves Transit. Your finance team requires cost attribution on all compute resources. You add these tags to the lab cluster configuration. Where do these tags appear after the cluster runs workloads?

options.label: In Azure cost management and billing reports, enabling spend attribution by project and cost center
As metadata columns automatically appended to every Delta table written by the cluster
In Unity Catalog data lineage graphs to track which cluster produced each output table
In Databricks audit logs as access-control events attached to each cluster start and stop

questions.explanation: Cluster tags propagate to Azure resource billing data. Teams use them to attribute cloud spend by environment, team, or cost center in Azure Cost Management. They do not affect permissions, table metadata, or lineage tracking.

questions.prompt: Your team must ingest JSON event files arriving continuously at ~1,000 files per minute from Azure Data Lake into a Delta table. Which ingestion approach is most appropriate and why?

options.label: Auto Loader with cloudFiles format — uses file notifications or incremental listing to track new files without rescanning the full directory each microbatch
COPY INTO — optimized for high-frequency streaming and tracks each file for exactly-once delivery
PySpark spark.read.json() in a scheduled Job — scales by parallelizing reads across Spark executors
Azure Data Factory Copy Activity — handles JSON natively and writes directly to Delta format without Databricks compute

questions.explanation: Auto Loader (cloudFiles) is designed for continuous file ingestion at scale. It tracks which files have been processed using Azure Event Grid notifications or incremental directory listing, avoiding expensive full-directory scans. COPY INTO is better suited for scheduled batch loads.

questions.prompt: Your Auto Loader pipeline has cloudFiles.inferColumnTypes enabled and a schemaLocation configured. After three months, source Parquet files begin including a new field temperature_c that was absent from the original schema. What does Auto Loader do on the next microbatch?

options.label: The pipeline fails immediately with a schema mismatch error and must be manually restarted with a schema reset flag
Detects the evolved schema, updates the checkpoint at schemaLocation, triggers a controlled stream restart to apply the new schema; prior rows receive NULL for the new column
Silently drops temperature_c to preserve backward schema compatibility with the existing Delta table
Promotes all existing columns to STRING to accommodate the new field without modifying the schema checkpoint

questions.explanation: Auto Loader detects schema evolution and updates the schema checkpoint. It raises a SchemaEvolutionException to trigger a controlled stream restart so the new schema is applied cleanly. After restart, existing rows get NULL for the new column and new rows include temperature_c.

questions.prompt: Your pipeline receives daily sales CSV files via COPY INTO. The source occasionally re-delivers the prior day's file with corrections using the same filename. What is the key limitation of COPY INTO when corrections arrive as re-delivered files with the same path?

options.label: COPY INTO re-reads all previously loaded files on every run, creating duplicates each time a file is re-delivered
COPY INTO cannot process CSV files from ADLS — Parquet or Delta format is required for cloud storage sources
COPY INTO tracks loaded files by path in the Delta transaction log; a re-delivered file with the same path is treated as already loaded and skipped, so corrections are silently ignored
COPY INTO requires a primary key column to detect corrections; without it the command is rejected at parse time

questions.explanation: COPY INTO maintains idempotency by tracking loaded file paths in the Delta transaction log. A corrected file reusing the same path is considered already loaded and skipped. For correction workflows, MERGE INTO is the appropriate approach as it can upsert based on a key.

questions.prompt: Your Spark Structured Streaming job aggregates click events into 5-minute tumbling windows. You add .withWatermark("event_time", "10 minutes") to handle late data. What does the 10-minute watermark specifically control?

options.label: The maximum delay between microbatches — if no new data arrives within 10 minutes the stream stops automatically
The checkpoint flush interval — state files older than 10 minutes are garbage-collected from the checkpoint directory
The trigger interval — the stream processes one microbatch every 10 minutes regardless of file arrival cadence
How long Spark retains intermediate aggregation state for open windows; events arriving more than 10 minutes past their window's close time are dropped

questions.explanation: A watermark tells Spark the maximum lateness it should tolerate. State for a 5-minute window is kept until the event-time clock advances past (window-end + 10 min). Events arriving after that threshold are dropped. The watermark also lets Spark safely clean up old state to bound memory usage.

questions.prompt: You are a data engineer at Solaris Energy building an Auto Loader pipeline to ingest turbine sensor CSV files. The pipeline runs successfully, but after adding 500 new files you observe that some files are processed twice. What is the most likely cause?

codeSnippet.code:
df_turbine = (spark.readStream
    .format("cloudFiles")
    .option("cloudFiles.format", "csv")
    .option("cloudFiles.schemaLocation",
            "/checkpoints/solaris/schema")
    .load("abfss://raw@solarisstorage.dfs.core.windows.net/turbines/"))

(df_turbine.writeStream
    .format("delta")
    .option("checkpointLocation",
            "/checkpoints/solaris/bronze")
    .trigger(availableNow=True)
    .start("abfss://bronze@solarisstorage.dfs.core.windows.net/turbines"))

options.label: trigger(availableNow=True) forces Auto Loader to replay all source files from the beginning on each run
cloudFiles.format = 'csv' does not support incremental file tracking; only JSON and Parquet formats maintain file state
Delta Lake does not support idempotent appends — duplicate files must be deduplicated manually with MERGE INTO downstream
The checkpointLocation was deleted or changed between runs, causing Auto Loader to lose track of which files were already processed

questions.explanation: Auto Loader tracks processed files using the checkpointLocation. If this path is deleted, moved, or changed between runs, Auto Loader loses its state and re-processes files it already loaded. trigger(availableNow=True) is safe and does not cause replays when the checkpoint is intact.

questions.prompt: You are a data engineer ingesting daily real estate listing CSV files into a bronze Delta table. A scheduled job runs this statement twice in the same day due to a retry. What happens to the data in bronze.real_estate_listings on the second run?

codeSnippet.code:
COPY INTO bronze.real_estate_listings
FROM 'abfss://raw@realestatestorage.dfs.core.windows.net/listings/2024/'
FILEFORMAT = CSV
FORMAT_OPTIONS (
    'header' = 'true',
    'inferSchema' = 'true'
);

options.label: Only files not yet successfully loaded are ingested; already-processed files are skipped, making COPY INTO idempotent
The second run truncates the target table and reloads all files from scratch
The second run raises a FilesAlreadyLoadedException and the job fails immediately
Duplicate rows are inserted because COPY INTO does not track previously loaded files

questions.explanation: COPY INTO tracks which files have been successfully loaded in the Delta transaction log. Running it again is safe — new files are ingested and already-loaded files are skipped. This idempotency makes it reliable for scheduled batch jobs with retry logic.

questions.prompt: You are a data engineer at Solaris Energy. Your Auto Loader stream writes parsed turbine sensor readings to a silver Delta table. The cluster restarts mid-batch. After recovery, you observe no duplicate rows and no data loss. What makes exactly-once delivery possible?

codeSnippet.code:
(df_parsed
    .writeStream
    .format("delta")
    .outputMode("append")
    .option("checkpointLocation",
            "/checkpoints/solaris/silver-turbines")
    .trigger(availableNow=True)
    .start("abfss://silver@solarisstorage.dfs.core.windows.net/turbines"))

options.label: trigger(availableNow=True) replays only the last incomplete batch and discards any partial writes on cluster recovery
checkpointLocation stores committed source offsets and processed file state so the stream resumes exactly where it left off without reprocessing or losing data
Delta Lake automatically locks the output path during recovery to prevent concurrent writes that could cause duplication
outputMode("append") deduplicates rows by matching them against existing Delta records on each restart

questions.explanation: The checkpointLocation persists stream progress — which source offsets and files were committed. On restart, Spark reads this state and continues from the last successful commit, delivering exactly-once semantics when combined with Delta Lake's transactional writes.

questions.prompt: You are a data engineer at a real estate analytics company joining df_listings (8M rows), df_agents (200K rows), and df_zip_codes (800 rows). You apply a broadcast hint only to df_zip_codes. Join time drops from 5 minutes to 22 seconds. Why does broadcasting only df_zip_codes give the best result?

codeSnippet.code:
from pyspark.sql.functions import broadcast

df_result = (df_listings
    .join(df_agents, on="agent_id", how="left")
    .join(broadcast(df_zip_codes), on="zip_code", how="left"))

options.label: Spark allows only one broadcast hint per query; df_zip_codes is selected because it has the fewest columns
Broadcasting requires Delta Lake format; df_agents is stored as Parquet and cannot be broadcast automatically
df_zip_codes fits in executor memory and is replicated to all workers, eliminating the shuffle of df_listings; broadcasting df_agents at 200K rows would risk executor OOM and negate the benefit
df_agents has a surrogate primary key enabling an optimized sort-merge strategy that is faster than broadcasting for medium-sized tables

questions.explanation: A broadcast join copies the small table to every executor so the large table never shuffles across the network. An 800-row lookup is safe and eliminates an expensive Exchange stage. Attempting to broadcast a 200K-row table risks out-of-memory errors on executors and can be slower than a sort-merge join.

questions.prompt: You are a data engineer at a real estate analytics firm producing a quarterly average listing-price report. After running this transformation, what is the shape of df_quarterly compared with the original df_listings?

codeSnippet.code:
df_quarterly = (df_listings
    .groupBy("city")
    .pivot("quarter", ["Q1", "Q2", "Q3", "Q4"])
    .agg({"list_price": "avg"}))

df_quarterly.show()

options.label: Same row count as df_listings — pivot is a display transformation that does not change DataFrame structure
One row per (city, quarter) pair — same granularity as the original, sorted by quarter
The DataFrame is transposed so city names become column headers and quarters become the row index
One row per unique city with four new columns Q1, Q2, Q3, Q4 each containing the average list price for that quarter

questions.explanation: Pivot rotates the distinct values of the pivot column (quarter) into separate output columns. The result has one row per city and four revenue columns (Q1–Q4) each containing the aggregated value, reducing row count compared to the original while widening the schema.

questions.prompt: The group analysts has SELECT on table main.sales.revenue. analysts is a child of group data_consumers, which also holds SELECT on the same table. You run REVOKE SELECT ON TABLE main.sales.revenue FROM GROUP analysts. Can members of analysts still query the table?

options.label: Yes — REVOKE removes only the direct grant from analysts; members who inherit SELECT through data_consumers retain access
No — REVOKE propagates transitively through parent groups and removes inherited access as well
No — Unity Catalog applies the most restrictive grant when a direct revoke conflicts with an inherited grant
Yes — but only until the next metastore sync, after which the inherited access is also revoked

questions.explanation: Revoking a privilege from a group removes only that direct grant. Users who belong to multiple groups retain access if another group still holds the privilege. Unity Catalog privilege evaluation is additive — the most permissive applicable grant wins.

questions.prompt: A service principal has SELECT on table prod.finance.invoices but no other Unity Catalog grants. It runs SELECT * FROM prod.finance.invoices and receives SCHEMA_NOT_FOUND. What privilege is missing?

options.label: Service principals cannot use SQL SELECT — they must call the Databricks REST API to read tables
USE CATALOG on prod and USE SCHEMA on prod.finance — without these the three-level namespace cannot be traversed
SELECT on a managed table requires a separate EXTERNAL LOCATION grant for the underlying cloud storage path
The SELECT grant must be approved by a workspace admin within 24 hours before it takes effect

questions.explanation: Unity Catalog namespace traversal requires USE CATALOG at the catalog level and USE SCHEMA at the schema level. Even with SELECT on the table, without these traversal privileges the SQL engine cannot resolve the fully qualified name.

A job compute cluster triggered per dashboard refresh
A single-node classic cluster with autoscaling disabled

questions.explanation: Serverless SQL warehouses are purpose-built for BI/SQL workloads: they start in seconds, scale automatically with concurrent query load, and require no cluster administration — Databricks manages the underlying compute. Classic clusters (all-purpose or job) require capacity planning and startup time that don't fit a sub-2-second, zero-ops dashboard requirement.

questions.prompt: A nightly ETL job processes between 10 GB and 500 GB depending on the day, and the team wants both cost efficiency and a fast cluster start. Given this cluster spec, what is the effect of the `instance_pool_id` field?

options.label: It caps the maximum autoscaling ceiling at the pool's idle instance count
It replaces the need for autoscale settings since the pool handles all scaling decisions
It draws VMs from a pre-warmed idle pool so the cluster starts in seconds instead of waiting for new VMs to provision from Azure
It forces the cluster to use spot/low-priority instances exclusively

questions.explanation: Instance pools keep a set of idle, ready-to-use VMs so clusters attached to the pool skip Azure VM provisioning time on start and autoscale-up events. Autoscale min/max_workers still control how many nodes the cluster requests — the pool just changes where those nodes come from, not the scaling logic itself.

questions.prompt: An existing Spark SQL and DataFrame-heavy ETL pipeline needs a performance boost with no code changes. The team enables Photon on the cluster. Which statement correctly describes what happens?

options.label: Photon replaces the Spark driver with a GPU-based scheduler, requiring GPU-enabled node types
Photon only accelerates RDD-based code and has no effect on DataFrame or SQL workloads
Photon must be paired with a downgrade to an older Databricks Runtime version to function
Photon is a native vectorized query engine that accelerates SQL and DataFrame operations on Parquet/Delta data without requiring any code rewrites

questions.explanation: Photon is a C++-based vectorized execution engine, API-compatible with Spark SQL/DataFrames. Enabling it (via a Photon-enabled runtime) speeds up eligible SQL and DataFrame operations transparently — no query or code changes are needed, and it doesn't require GPU hardware.

questions.prompt: A scheduled job runs on a job cluster that is created fresh for every run and terminates afterward. The job requires `great_expectations==0.18.7`. A developer tests interactively with `%pip install great_expectations==0.18.7` in a notebook and it works. Why will the scheduled job still fail with `ModuleNotFoundError`?

options.label: %pip install libraries are notebook-session-scoped; a new job cluster spins up without that session state, so the library isn't installed unless it's added as a cluster or job-level library
%pip only works on all-purpose clusters and is silently ignored on any job cluster
great_expectations is incompatible with any Databricks Runtime version
%pip installs are workspace-wide but require an admin to approve each package before jobs can use them

questions.explanation: Notebook-scoped `%pip install` libraries live only in that notebook's Python session. A job cluster is provisioned fresh for the scheduled run and has no memory of prior interactive sessions. To make a library available to a job reliably, install it as a cluster library (UI/Libraries API) or declare it in the job/task's library list so it's installed as part of cluster startup.

codeSnippet.code:
# Works fine when run interactively in a notebook:
%pip install great_expectations==0.18.7

# But the scheduled Job fails with ModuleNotFoundError

questions.prompt: A workspace admin wants the `data-engineers` group to be able to attach notebooks to a shared cluster and view its Spark UI, but must prevent them from restarting the cluster or editing its configuration (which could disrupt other teams' running jobs). Which cluster permission level should be granted?

options.label: CAN MANAGE
CAN ATTACH TO
CAN RESTART
Workspace admin role, scoped to that cluster only

questions.explanation: Azure Databricks cluster permissions have three levels: CAN ATTACH TO (attach notebooks/run commands, view Spark UI — no restart or edit), CAN RESTART (adds restart/terminate), and CAN MANAGE (full control including edit, permissions, and delete). CAN ATTACH TO is the least-privilege option that satisfies the requirement.

questions.prompt: A company needs strict isolation between dev, staging, and prod data — including separate access-control boundaries and the ability to promote objects between environments without renaming everything. Which naming/isolation strategy best fits Unity Catalog's model?

options.label: One catalog for the whole company, with schema name prefixes like dev_sales, stg_sales, prod_sales
One schema per environment inside a single catalog, relying on table-level grants for isolation
Separate catalogs per environment (e.g. dev, staging, prod), each containing the same schema names underneath
A single catalog and schema, isolating environments purely through workspace-level network rules

questions.explanation: Catalog is the top-level container and primary isolation/access-control boundary in Unity Catalog. Modeling environments as separate catalogs (dev/staging/prod) with identical schema structure underneath gives clean privilege boundaries, simple environment promotion (same relative paths), and avoids leaking permissions across environments the way schema- or table-level naming conventions inside one catalog would.

questions.prompt: You need every managed table created under a new `prod_sales` catalog to store its underlying data in a dedicated ADLS Gen2 container, separate from other catalogs. Which statement achieves this?

options.label: It creates the catalog but storage location is ignored — Unity Catalog always uses the workspace's root storage for managed tables
It makes every table in the catalog an external table pointing at that container
MANAGED LOCATION is only valid on CREATE SCHEMA, not CREATE CATALOG, so this statement fails
It sets the default storage location for managed tables/schemas in this catalog; schemas can still override it with their own MANAGED LOCATION

questions.explanation: MANAGED LOCATION on CREATE CATALOG sets the default storage root that managed schemas/tables in that catalog inherit unless overridden. Unity Catalog supports specifying managed storage at the metastore, catalog, or schema level, with the more specific level taking precedence — giving isolation per catalog without forcing every table to be external.

codeSnippet.code:
CREATE CATALOG IF NOT EXISTS prod_sales
MANAGED LOCATION 'abfss://prod-sales@mystorageacct.dfs.core.windows.net/';

questions.prompt: The finance team's schema must keep its managed table data in a separate storage container from the rest of the `prod_sales` catalog, for a compliance requirement specific to that team. What is the correct approach?

options.label: This overrides the catalog-level managed location for this schema only; managed tables created in prod_sales.finance will use the schema's storage path instead of the catalog default
This is invalid — all schemas in a catalog must share the catalog's managed location
This creates an external schema, meaning every table inside it must also declare its own LOCATION
The MANAGED LOCATION clause only affects volumes created in the schema, not tables

questions.explanation: Unity Catalog resolves managed storage location hierarchically: schema-level MANAGED LOCATION overrides the catalog default, which itself overrides the metastore root. This lets a single catalog host schemas with different storage/compliance boundaries without needing separate catalogs.

codeSnippet.code:
CREATE SCHEMA IF NOT EXISTS prod_sales.finance
MANAGED LOCATION 'abfss://finance-restricted@mystorageacct.dfs.core.windows.net/';

questions.prompt: A data science team needs to read and write arbitrary unstructured files (images, PDFs) from Databricks notebooks and external tools, governed by Unity Catalog, without modeling the files as a table. What should they create?

options.label: A managed table with a single BINARY column
A Unity Catalog volume, which governs access to non-tabular files via a catalog/schema-scoped file path
A DBFS mount point, since volumes cannot store binary files
An external location with no schema association

questions.explanation: Volumes are the Unity Catalog object for governing non-tabular data (arbitrary files) under the same catalog.schema.volume namespace and permission model as tables, accessible via a standard file path. They're the recommended replacement for ungoverned DBFS mounts when files don't fit a table structure.

codeSnippet.code:
CREATE VOLUME IF NOT EXISTS prod_sales.finance.contract_scans
COMMENT 'PDF contract scans for OCR pipeline';

questions.prompt: Five dashboards run the same expensive multi-join aggregation query against a 2 TB fact table every few minutes, driving up compute cost and query latency. The result set only needs to reflect data as of the last hourly ETL run. What's the best fix?

options.label: Replace it with a regular VIEW, which caches results automatically
There is no way to avoid recomputation short of manually writing to a new table with a scheduled job
Use a materialized view: the aggregation is precomputed and refreshed on a schedule, so dashboards read a small precomputed table instead of recomputing the join/aggregation each time
Materialized views recompute on every query just like regular views, so this wouldn't help

questions.explanation: Unlike a regular view (computed at query time on every read), a materialized view precomputes and stores its result, refreshing on a defined schedule or trigger. This is exactly suited to expensive, repeatedly-queried aggregations where slightly-stale (hourly) data is acceptable — dashboards then read a small precomputed table instead of re-running the join.

codeSnippet.code:
CREATE MATERIALIZED VIEW prod_sales.gold.hourly_revenue_summary
SCHEDULE CRON '0 0 * * * ?'
AS
SELECT region, product_category, SUM(revenue) AS total_revenue
FROM prod_sales.silver.orders
JOIN prod_sales.silver.products USING (product_id)
GROUP BY region, product_category;

questions.prompt: Analysts need to run SQL joins between Databricks tables and live data in an external Snowflake database, without building an ETL pipeline to copy the Snowflake data into Databricks first. What Unity Catalog feature enables this?

options.label: Delta Sharing, which requires the Snowflake side to export a share first
Auto Loader, pointed at Snowflake's internal stage
A materialized view that pulls from an external table nightly
Lakehouse Federation: a CONNECTION plus FOREIGN CATALOG lets Databricks query the external Snowflake database directly, governed by Unity Catalog, with no data copy

questions.explanation: Lakehouse Federation lets Unity Catalog register a CONNECTION to an external system (Snowflake, SQL Server, MySQL, PostgreSQL, etc.) and expose it as a FOREIGN CATALOG, so users can query external data directly through Databricks compute — governed like any other UC object — without ETL-ing it in first.

questions.prompt: Business users ask an AI/BI Genie space "what were our top customers last quarter?" and it repeatedly generates SQL that joins the wrong tables, because "customer" is ambiguous between a `billing_account` table and a `end_user` table. The underlying data and permissions are correct. What should the Genie space owner do?

options.label: Add Genie instructions that define business terms (e.g. "customer" = billing_account) and specify preferred join paths/sample queries, giving Genie the context to generate correct SQL
Rebuild the tables with clearer column names, since Genie instructions cannot influence query generation
Grant Genie's service principal owner-level privileges on both tables so it can infer the right one
Disable natural-language mode and require all users to write raw SQL instead

questions.explanation: AI/BI Genie spaces support curated "instructions" — business-term definitions, preferred join logic, and example question/SQL pairs — that ground the natural-language-to-SQL generation in the team's actual semantics. This directly resolves ambiguous terminology issues without touching schema or permissions, which don't affect Genie's query-generation logic.

questions.prompt: A team is migrating a legacy ADLS Gen2 dataset into Unity Catalog. They must be able to remove and recreate the table definition during schema iteration without ever risking deletion of the underlying Parquet files, since other non-Databricks tools also read them directly. Which DDL approach is correct?

options.label: This creates a managed table; removing the table will delete the underlying files regardless of the LOCATION clause
This creates an external table; Unity Catalog only manages the metadata/catalog entry, so removing the table leaves the underlying files untouched
The LOCATION clause is only cosmetic for managed tables and has no effect on deletion behavior
External tables cannot be created this way; they require a separate statement

questions.explanation: Specifying LOCATION on CREATE TABLE makes it an external table: Unity Catalog governs access and metadata but does not own the data's lifecycle. Removing the table deletes only the catalog entry, leaving files at that path untouched — exactly what's needed when other tools depend on those files directly. Managed tables (no LOCATION) behave oppositely and delete the underlying data when removed.

codeSnippet.code: CREATE TABLE prod_sales.bronze.legacy_orders USING PARQUET LOCATION 'abfss://legacy@mystorageacct.dfs.core.windows.net/orders/'

questions.prompt: You need to grant the `analytics_team` group SELECT access to every current and future table in the `prod_sales.gold` schema, without re-running a grant every time a new table is added. Which approach is correct in Unity Catalog?

options.label: This is sufficient on its own — schema-level grants automatically cover all current and future tables
SELECT cannot be granted at the schema level; it must be granted per table
Grants in Unity Catalog only apply to objects that exist at grant time; new tables need either a fresh grant or a schema-level default/future-object grant policy to be covered automatically
Group-based grants are not supported; only individual users and service principals can be granted privileges

questions.explanation: A schema-level GRANT SELECT applies to objects that exist at the time it's issued. Unity Catalog does not retroactively or automatically extend that grant to tables created afterward unless you use a mechanism intended for future objects; otherwise each new table needs its own grant (or a repeated schema grant). Group-based grants to principals like `analytics_team` are fully supported.

codeSnippet.code: GRANT SELECT ON SCHEMA prod_sales.gold TO `analytics_team`

questions.prompt: A `customers` table contains a `ssn` column that only the compliance team should see, and EU-based analysts should only see rows where `region = 'EU'`. Both restrictions must be enforced centrally so every query — notebook, SQL warehouse, or BI tool — respects them automatically. What's the right Unity Catalog mechanism?

options.label: Create separate physical tables per region and per privilege level, and grant access to the matching copy
Rely on each BI tool's own row-level security feature, configured separately per tool
Encrypt the ssn column client-side and distribute decryption keys only to compliance team laptops
Apply a column mask function to `ssn` and a row filter function on `region`, both defined once on the table in Unity Catalog

questions.explanation: Unity Catalog supports column masks (functions that redact/transform a column's value based on the querying user's group membership) and row filters (functions that restrict which rows are visible), both defined once at the table level. Because enforcement happens in Unity Catalog itself, it applies uniformly across every compute path — notebooks, SQL warehouses, and connected BI tools — with no per-tool configuration.

questions.prompt: A notebook needs a database password to connect to an on-prem SQL Server via JDBC. The password is stored in Azure Key Vault. The team wants to avoid ever pasting the raw secret into notebook code or job configuration. What should they do?

options.label: Create an Azure Key Vault-backed secret scope in Databricks, then reference secrets via dbutils.secrets.get() as shown — the raw value is never displayed and is redacted from notebook output/logs
Copy the secret value into a Databricks widget default value so it's easy to reuse across notebooks
Store the password as a cluster environment variable in plain text, since cluster configs are workspace-private
Secrets can only be accessed by Databricks-native secret scopes; Key Vault-backed scopes are not supported

questions.explanation: Databricks supports Azure Key Vault-backed secret scopes: once configured, `dbutils.secrets.get()` retrieves the value at runtime without the code ever containing the raw secret, and Databricks automatically redacts secret values from notebook output and logs (printing REDACTED instead).

codeSnippet.code: jdbc_password = dbutils.secrets.get(scope="kv-onprem-sql", key="sql-password")

questions.prompt: A Lakeflow Job runs unattended every night and needs to read/write Unity Catalog tables. The security team requires that the job's identity be independent of any individual employee's account, so access isn't revoked when that employee leaves the company. What should own and run the job?

options.label: The data engineer's personal Azure AD account, since personal accounts have the broadest default permissions
A Microsoft Entra ID service principal, created specifically for this job and granted only the Unity Catalog privileges it needs
A shared team login shared informally among engineers via a password manager
A personal access token (PAT) generated from any admin's account, rotated manually every 90 days

questions.explanation: Service principals are non-human identities meant exactly for unattended workloads like scheduled jobs: they're independent of any individual's employment status, can be scoped to least-privilege Unity Catalog grants, and are the recommended pattern over running jobs under personal accounts or shared credentials.

questions.prompt: A Databricks notebook needs to read files from an ADLS Gen2 storage account. The security team's policy forbids storing any storage account keys or SAS tokens anywhere in workspace configuration. Which authentication approach satisfies this policy?

options.label: Hardcode the storage account access key in the notebook, since notebooks are only visible to authorized workspace users
Generate a long-lived SAS token and store it in a workspace notebook parameter

Use a managed identity (assigned to the Databricks access connector or compute) that Azure AD authenticates automatically, with RBAC roles granted on the storage account — no keys or tokens stored anywhere
Mount the storage account using the account key via dbutils.fs.mount, which encrypts the key automatically at rest

questions.explanation: Managed identities let Azure AD authenticate the Databricks access connector (or compute) directly against the storage account via RBAC role assignments (e.g., Storage Blob Data Reader). No credential — key, SAS token, or secret — needs to be stored or managed anywhere, satisfying a no-stored-keys policy while still allowing fine-grained, revocable access.

questions.prompt: A new analyst joins the data team and needs to understand what the `net_revenue` column in `prod_sales.gold.orders` actually represents — whether it's before or after refunds — without pinging the original author. What should have been set up in advance to make this self-service?

options.label: A README file stored separately in a Confluence page linked from the team wiki
A Slack channel dedicated to answering schema questions
Naming the column net_revenue_after_refunds instead, since column names alone are sufficient documentation
Column and table comments/descriptions set via Unity Catalog DDL (or Catalog Explorer), which surface directly in the catalog's metadata for anyone browsing the table

questions.explanation: Unity Catalog lets you attach persistent comments/descriptions to catalogs, schemas, tables, and individual columns. These surface directly in Catalog Explorer and query tools, making tribal knowledge discoverable in place rather than relying on external docs or asking a person — exactly the self-service data discovery UC governance is meant to enable.

questions.prompt: A company has 40 tables tagged with sensitivity levels (`pii`, `internal`, `public`) across multiple catalogs. Security wants one rule that says "only members of the security-cleared group can read any table tagged pii" — enforced automatically as new pii-tagged tables appear, without editing grants table by table. What should they implement?

options.label: Attribute-based access control (ABAC): a policy that references the pii tag, so any object carrying that tag is governed by the rule automatically, including new ones
A saved SQL query that lists all pii tables, reviewed manually each week
Individual GRANT/REVOKE statements re-run every time a new table is created
Row filters applied to every table, keyed on a hardcoded list of table names

questions.explanation: Attribute-based access control (ABAC) in Unity Catalog lets you write policies against tags rather than individual object names. Because the policy targets the tag itself, any object — including ones created later — carrying that tag is automatically governed, eliminating the need for per-table grant maintenance.

questions.prompt: Support engineers need to see customer support tickets including the customer's email address, but must see only the last 4 digits of any stored payment card number. The underlying table has both columns. Which combination of governance features applies here?

options.label: A row filter on the email column and a column mask on the card number column
A column mask function on the card number column that redacts all but the last 4 digits for the support group, while other columns remain visible to them as normal
Two separate physical tables, one with the full card number and one without
Row-level security keyed on the customer's card number value

questions.explanation: This scenario needs column-level redaction, not row filtering — support engineers should see every row (row filters restrict which rows are visible, not appropriate here) but a transformed version of one column. A column mask function conditionally applies masking logic (e.g., show only last 4 digits) based on the querying user's group membership, leaving other columns like email untouched.

questions.prompt: A compliance requirement states that raw clickstream event data must not be queryable after 13 months, but the aggregated monthly summary tables derived from it can be kept indefinitely. How should this be implemented in Unity Catalog / Delta Lake?

options.label: Manually delete the raw table every 13 months via an ad-hoc script run by an engineer
Set a single workspace-wide retention setting that applies identically to every table, raw or aggregated

Apply a data retention policy to the raw events table (e.g., a scheduled process using Delta's time-based deletion/VACUUM-aligned retention) while leaving the aggregate tables unmanaged by that policy
Rely on Delta Lake's default VACUUM schedule, which automatically enforces business-level retention requirements out of the box

questions.explanation: Retention policies need to be scoped per table/object based on business requirements — raw and aggregate tables here have different lifecycles. Delta Lake's default VACUUM only cleans up stale file versions for time-travel purposes; it does not enforce business retention SLAs on its own, so a deliberate retention policy/process must be defined for tables where old data must be purged.

questions.prompt: A data engineer wants to understand which downstream dashboards would break if column `customer_id` were renamed in `prod_sales.silver.customers`, before making the change. Where should they look?

options.label: The cluster event log, which records every read/write operation against the table
The audit log, filtered to GRANT/REVOKE events on this table
There is no built-in way to trace this; it must be tracked manually in a spreadsheet
Catalog Explorer's lineage graph, which shows upstream/downstream tables, notebooks, jobs, and dashboards derived from this table/column

questions.explanation: Unity Catalog automatically captures data lineage — tracking dependencies between tables, columns, notebooks, jobs, dashboards, and other assets — and surfaces it visually in Catalog Explorer, including column-level lineage. This is exactly the tool for impact analysis before a breaking schema change, rather than the audit log (which tracks access/permission events) or manual tracking.

questions.prompt: A security audit asks: "Show every user who queried the `prod_sales.gold.executive_comp` table in the last 90 days, and every permission change made to it." Where does this information come from in an Azure Databricks / Unity Catalog deployment?

options.label: Unity Catalog audit logs delivered to Azure (via diagnostic settings/Log Analytics), which capture query access events and privilege change events at the object level
The Spark UI's SQL tab, which retains query history indefinitely for all users
Cluster-level init script logs
There's no way to retroactively audit this; access must be logged manually by each user

questions.explanation: Unity Catalog emits detailed audit logs — including table access events and privilege/grant changes — that can be routed to Azure Monitor/Log Analytics via diagnostic settings for retention, querying, and compliance reporting. This is the authoritative source for "who accessed what, and what permissions changed," not the Spark UI (ephemeral, per-cluster) or init script logs.

questions.prompt: Your company wants to give an external partner organization read access to three specific Delta tables, refreshed continuously, without giving them a Databricks workspace login, a copy of your storage credentials, or requiring them to run Databricks at all. What should you design?

options.label: Export the tables to CSV and email them a new file weekly
A Delta Sharing share containing exactly those three tables, granted to a recipient defined by the partner's sharing identifier — no workspace account or credential sharing required
Create a guest workspace account for the partner with SELECT grants on the three tables
Give the partner the storage account's SAS token scoped to the three tables' underlying files

questions.explanation: Delta Sharing is Databricks' open protocol for sharing live data across organizational and platform boundaries without copying it or requiring the recipient to use Databricks. A secure share can be scoped to exactly the needed tables and granted to an external recipient, avoiding the security and operational downsides of guest accounts, raw credential sharing, or manual file exports.

questions.prompt: A source system exports full-file CSV snapshots nightly (no change tracking available), while another source is a transactional database with a native CDC feed available. Both need to land in Unity Catalog. Which statement about designing the ingestion logic is correct?

options.label: The CSV source is best handled as a full/batch extraction with file-based ingestion (e.g. Auto Loader), while the CDC-capable source should use change-based extraction to avoid reprocessing entire tables
Both sources should use the exact same extraction pattern for consistency, ignoring what each source system actually offers
CSV files cannot be ingested incrementally under any circumstances, so they must always be loaded as one giant historical batch
CDC feeds should be treated as full snapshots and reloaded in their entirety on every run to guarantee correctness

questions.explanation: Ingestion design should match what each source can actually provide: a snapshot-only CSV export is naturally suited to file-based batch/incremental ingestion (e.g. Auto Loader tracking new files), while a CDC-capable source should be ingested via its change feed so only deltas are processed — avoiding full reprocessing and reducing cost/latency.

questions.prompt: You need to ingest data from Salesforce, SQL Server, and a set of REST APIs into Unity Catalog. Salesforce and SQL Server are both supported natively; the REST APIs are bespoke internal services with custom auth. Which ingestion tool choice best fits each?

options.label: Use custom notebooks with Spark/Python for everything, since it's the most flexible option regardless of source type

Use Lakeflow Connect for the natively supported Salesforce/SQL Server connectors (managed, low-maintenance ingestion), and custom notebooks (or Azure Data Factory) for the bespoke REST APIs that need custom auth/logic
Use Azure Data Factory exclusively, since Lakeflow Connect cannot ingest from SaaS applications like Salesforce
Use Lakeflow Connect for the REST APIs too, since it supports arbitrary custom HTTP endpoints out of the box

questions.explanation: Lakeflow Connect provides managed, low-code connectors for common enterprise sources (Salesforce, SQL Server, and other SaaS/database systems), reducing operational overhead versus hand-rolled ingestion. For bespoke internal REST APIs with custom auth/logic that no managed connector covers, notebooks (or orchestrated via Azure Data Factory) remain the right tool — matching ingestion tool choice to what each source actually needs.

questions.prompt: A fraud-detection use case needs to react to new transactions within seconds of them occurring. A separate monthly financial reconciliation report only needs data as of the end of each day. Both read from the same underlying transaction source. What data loading method should each use?

options.label: Both should use streaming, since streaming is strictly better than batch in every scenario
Both should use batch loading once per month to minimize compute cost

Fraud detection should use streaming ingestion (low latency, continuous processing); the monthly reconciliation report can use batch ingestion (e.g. a daily scheduled job), since near-real-time freshness isn't required
Loading method should be identical for both since they share the same source table

questions.explanation: Loading method should be chosen per use case's latency requirement, not per source. Streaming (e.g. Structured Streaming/Auto Loader) fits low-latency needs like fraud detection where seconds matter. Batch loading is more cost-efficient and operationally simpler when eventual, periodic freshness (like end-of-day) is sufficient — as with the monthly reconciliation report.

questions.prompt: A pipeline lands raw JSON logs, then needs to support fast MERGE-based upserts, ACID transactions, and time travel for auditing, while remaining fully compatible with the Databricks lakehouse ecosystem. Which table format should the curated (silver/gold) layers use?

options.label: Raw JSON, kept as-is through every layer to avoid conversion overhead
CSV, since it's universally readable by any tool
Plain Parquet without a transaction log, since Parquet alone provides ACID guarantees
Delta Lake (built on Parquet), which natively provides ACID transactions, efficient MERGE/upserts, and time travel

questions.explanation: Delta Lake is the table format purpose-built for exactly these requirements: ACID transactions, efficient MERGE for upserts, and time travel via its transaction log — layered on top of Parquet's columnar storage. JSON and CSV are fine as raw landing formats but lack these transactional guarantees; plain Parquet without a transaction log also lacks ACID/time-travel support on its own.

questions.prompt: A 5 TB events table is queried almost exclusively with filters on `event_date`, and daily batch jobs only touch the current day's partition. Query performance on old, unfiltered full-table scans is not a concern. Which partitioning approach is most appropriate?

options.label: Partition by event_date, since queries consistently filter on it and daily jobs naturally align with day-sized partitions, enabling partition pruning
No partitioning at all, relying purely on file statistics
Partition by a random hash column to maximize write parallelism regardless of query patterns
Partition by every high-cardinality column in the table to maximize granularity

questions.explanation: Partitioning should align with dominant query filter patterns and natural write/access granularity. Here, queries consistently filter on event_date and jobs process one day at a time, so partitioning by event_date enables partition pruning (skipping irrelevant files) and matches operational patterns. Over-partitioning on high-cardinality columns instead creates the classic 'small files' problem and hurts performance.

questions.prompt: A `customers` dimension table needs to preserve full history of address changes for accurate historical reporting (e.g. "what region was this customer in when they placed order #4521?"), while still supporting an easy "current address" lookup. Which SCD (slowly changing dimension) type fits best?

options.label: SCD Type 1 — overwrite the old value with the new one
SCD Type 2 — insert a new row for each change, with effective/expiry dates (or a current-flag) so historical joins resolve to the address that was valid at that point in time
SCD Type 0 — never allow the address to change once set
Store only the current address and reconstruct history from application logs on demand

questions.explanation: SCD Type 2 preserves full history by inserting a new versioned row per change (typically with effective_date/end_date or a current flag), which is exactly what's needed to answer point-in-time historical questions correctly. SCD Type 1 (overwrite) would lose the historical address entirely, breaking the "region at time of order" use case.

questions.prompt: A gold-layer table currently stores one row per individual transaction. A finance dashboard only ever needs daily totals per store, and the transaction-level detail is never queried directly by that dashboard. What granularity decision would most improve the dashboard's efficiency?

options.label: Keep transaction-level granularity everywhere and let the dashboard's BI tool aggregate on every query
Delete the transaction-level table entirely once the aggregate exists, since finer granularity is never useful
Create a coarser-grained aggregate table (or materialized view) at store/day granularity specifically for the dashboard, while retaining the transaction-level table for use cases that need it
Increase granularity further by adding an hour-of-day dimension, since more granularity always improves performance

questions.explanation: Granularity should be chosen per consumer's actual query pattern. A dashboard that only needs store/day totals benefits from a pre-aggregated table at that granularity (avoiding repeated aggregation of transaction-level data on every query), while other consumers that need transaction-level detail still have that table available — granularity choices aren't one-size-fits-all across a whole platform.

questions.prompt: Auditors need to be able to answer "what did the customer's loyalty tier look like as of any date in the last 3 years", not just today. The team decides to build a table that records every tier value along with the time range it was valid. What is this pattern called, and what should the table include?

options.label: A snapshot table containing only today's tier per customer, refreshed daily
A materialized view recomputed from scratch on every query, since materialized views inherently store full history
A simple UPDATE-in-place table, since Delta Lake's time travel alone satisfies this requirement without any schema design
A temporal (history) table: one row per tier-change event per customer, with valid_from/valid_to timestamps, enabling point-in-time reconstruction for any historical date

questions.explanation: A temporal/history table explicitly models validity periods (valid_from/valid_to) per record version, letting queries reconstruct "what was true as of date X" without relying on Delta's time-travel feature (which reflects table snapshot history, not necessarily business-meaningful validity periods, and has retention limits). This is the standard pattern for long-term point-in-time auditability.

questions.prompt: A 10 TB table is frequently filtered on a high-cardinality `user_id` column and a medium-cardinality `country` column, but data arrival order makes traditional static partitioning by either column impractical (skewed, constantly-changing value distributions). The team also wants to avoid manually running maintenance commands after every load. What clustering strategy fits best?

options.label: Liquid clustering on (user_id, country), which incrementally and automatically reorganizes data by clustering keys without requiring rigid partition definitions or manual OPTIMIZE scheduling for rebalancing
Traditional Hive-style static partitioning by user_id, accepting the skew
Z-ordering only, which requires no clustering key definition and works automatically on every column
No clustering strategy is needed since Delta Lake automatically optimizes file layout with zero configuration

questions.explanation: Liquid clustering is designed for exactly this case: high/varying-cardinality columns where static partitioning causes skew or too many small partitions. It clusters data incrementally as it's written and adapts over time, reducing the need for manual OPTIMIZE/Z-order maintenance while still enabling efficient file pruning on the clustering keys.

questions.prompt: A team is registering a table backed by data another department already produces and owns in their own ADLS Gen2 container. The team must never accidentally delete that department's underlying files, even if their own table is dropped for cleanup. Which table type should they create, and why?

options.label: A managed table, because managed tables are always safer for shared data
An unmanaged (external) table pointing at the other department's storage path — Unity Catalog governs metadata/access only, so dropping the table never deletes the underlying files
Either type works identically in terms of data deletion risk
A managed table with a manual reminder process to back up the data before any drop operation

questions.explanation: This is the core distinction between managed and unmanaged (external) tables: dropping a managed table deletes its underlying data, while dropping an unmanaged/external table only removes the catalog entry — the files remain exactly as they were. For data owned and physically managed by another team, external/unmanaged is the safe choice.

questions.prompt: You need to stand up a production-grade ingestion pipeline from Salesforce into Unity Catalog with minimal custom code, automatic schema evolution handling, and built-in incremental extraction — without writing a custom connector. Which approach fits?

options.label: A hand-written Python notebook using the raw Salesforce REST API and manual pagination/state tracking
Spark Structured Streaming reading directly from Salesforce's database files
Lakeflow Connect's managed Salesforce connector, configured to run in batch or streaming mode as needed
COPY INTO pointed at the Salesforce web UI export URL

questions.explanation: Lakeflow Connect provides managed, low-code connectors for common SaaS/enterprise sources like Salesforce, handling extraction, incremental/CDC-style updates, and schema evolution with minimal custom code — supporting both batch and streaming ingestion modes. Hand-rolled REST integrations require far more maintenance for the same outcome.

questions.prompt: A data engineer wants a notebook cell that ingests new files from a cloud storage path incrementally on each run, without manually tracking which files were already processed, and that stays robust to new files continuously arriving. Which pattern accomplishes this within a notebook?

options.label: This re-reads every file in the directory on every run, since readStream always performs a full scan
The checkpointLocation is optional decoration and has no effect on which files get reprocessed
This pattern only works for Parquet files, not JSON

This uses Auto Loader (cloudFiles) with trigger(availableNow=True), which incrementally discovers and processes only new files each run using its own file-tracking state, then stops — giving batch-like scheduling with streaming-style incremental file tracking

questions.explanation: Auto Loader (cloudFiles format) incrementally and efficiently discovers new files in cloud storage using its own scalable file-tracking state (backed by the checkpoint location), avoiding full directory listings on every run. `trigger(availableNow=True)` processes all currently available new data then stops — a common pattern for running incremental ingestion on a schedule (e.g., inside a notebook task) rather than as an always-on stream.

codeSnippet.code:
df = (spark.readStream
      .format("cloudFiles")
      .option("cloudFiles.format", "json")
      .option("cloudFiles.schemaLocation", "/mnt/schemas/orders")
      .load("/mnt/raw/orders/"))

(df.writeStream
   .option("checkpointLocation", "/mnt/checkpoints/orders")
   .trigger(availableNow=True)
   .table("prod_sales.bronze.orders"))

questions.prompt: A gold table needs to be rebuilt every night from a large staging table using a single, all-at-once SQL statement (not incremental appends), where the output table's schema should exactly match the SELECT's output. Which SQL method fits?

options.label: CREATE OR REPLACE TABLE ... AS (CRAS) atomically replaces the table's data and schema with the query result each run, which is exactly suited for a full nightly rebuild
COPY INTO, since it's the only method that supports SELECT-based transformations
MERGE INTO with no matching condition, which behaves identically to a full table replace
INSERT INTO, since it automatically clears the target table before every load

questions.explanation: CREATE OR REPLACE TABLE ... AS SELECT (sometimes called CRAS) atomically swaps the table's contents and schema with a query's output — ideal for full, deterministic nightly rebuilds where you always want the target to exactly reflect the latest computed result. COPY INTO is for incrementally loading files into an existing table, not query-driven full rebuilds; INSERT INTO appends rather than replacing.

codeSnippet.code:
CREATE OR REPLACE TABLE prod_sales.gold.daily_summary AS
SELECT store_id, order_date, SUM(amount) AS total_sales
FROM prod_sales.silver.orders
GROUP BY store_id, order_date

questions.prompt: A source SQL Server table emits inserts, updates, and deletes that need to be reflected in a Unity Catalog Delta table with minimal latency and without reprocessing the full source table each time. Which ingestion approach directly addresses this requirement?

options.label: A nightly CREATE OR REPLACE TABLE ... AS SELECT * FROM the full source table
Consuming a change data capture (CDC) feed from the source and applying inserts/updates/deletes incrementally (e.g. via MERGE or APPLY CHANGES INTO in a Declarative Pipeline)
A one-time COPY INTO run when the table is first created, with no further updates
Periodically dropping and recreating the entire target table from a fresh export

questions.explanation: CDC feeds capture row-level insert/update/delete events from the source as they happen. Applying them incrementally — via MERGE logic or Lakeflow Declarative Pipelines' APPLY CHANGES INTO — keeps the target table current with low latency and without reprocessing the entire source table on every run, unlike full-refresh approaches (CRAS or drop/recreate).

questions.prompt: A team needs to compute a running 5-minute windowed aggregate over an unbounded stream of IoT sensor readings, with results updating continuously as new data arrives, and must correctly handle late-arriving events within a bounded delay. Which technology is purpose-built for this?

options.label: A batch job run every 5 minutes using CREATE OR REPLACE TABLE, since batch and streaming produce identical results for windowed aggregates
COPY INTO with a WHERE clause filtering the last 5 minutes of data
Spark Structured Streaming, whose windowed aggregation and watermarking (withWatermark) natively support continuous windowed computation with bounded handling of late data
Auto Loader alone, without Structured Streaming, since Auto Loader natively performs windowed aggregation

questions.explanation: Spark Structured Streaming provides native windowed aggregation (`window()`) and watermarking (`withWatermark`) to bound how long the engine waits for late-arriving events before finalizing a window — exactly the semantics needed for continuous, correctness-aware streaming aggregates. Auto Loader is a file-ingestion source, not an aggregation engine; it's typically used as the read side feeding into Structured Streaming logic like this.

codeSnippet.code:
from pyspark.sql.functions import window, avg

(spark.readStream.table("prod_iot.bronze.sensor_readings")
  .withWatermark("event_time", "10 minutes")
  .groupBy(window("event_time", "5 minutes"), "sensor_id")
  .agg(avg("temperature").alias("avg_temp"))
  .writeStream
  .outputMode("append")
  .table("prod_iot.silver.temp_5min_avg"))

questions.prompt: A team needs to ingest a continuous stream of clickstream events published to an Azure Event Hubs namespace, landing them into a bronze Delta table in near-real-time. Which approach is correct?

options.label: Export Event Hubs data to CSV files hourly and use COPY INTO, since Event Hubs cannot be read directly by Spark
Use Auto Loader's cloudFiles format directly against the Event Hubs namespace endpoint
Event Hubs data must first be manually copied into ADLS Gen2 before Databricks can process it
Use the Structured Streaming Event Hubs connector to read the stream directly, then write it into the bronze Delta table with writeStream

questions.explanation: Azure Databricks reads Event Hubs streams directly via the Structured Streaming Event Hubs connector (`format("eventhubs")`), enabling low-latency, near-real-time ingestion straight into a bronze Delta table with writeStream — no intermediate file export or manual copy step is needed. Auto Loader/cloudFiles is for cloud object storage, not message streaming services like Event Hubs.

questions.prompt: A team wants a declarative ingestion pipeline where they only describe the desired bronze/silver/gold tables and transformations, and the platform automatically manages incremental file discovery, dependency ordering, and orchestration — rather than hand-writing Structured Streaming checkpoint/trigger logic themselves. What should they use?

options.label: Lakeflow Spark Declarative Pipelines (using Auto Loader as the ingestion source within @dlt.table definitions), which manages orchestration, incremental processing, and dependency graphs declaratively
A raw Structured Streaming job with manually configured checkpoints, which is the only way to get incremental ingestion
Azure Data Factory copy activities exclusively, since Databricks has no declarative pipeline concept
A single monolithic notebook using dbutils.notebook.run() to chain bronze/silver/gold steps

questions.explanation: Lakeflow Spark Declarative Pipelines (formerly Delta Live Tables) let engineers declare table definitions and transformations, with the platform handling incremental processing, task orchestration, and dependency resolution automatically. Auto Loader is commonly used as the ingestion source inside these pipelines, removing the need to hand-manage Structured Streaming checkpoint/trigger plumbing directly.

questions.prompt: Before designing transformations for a newly onboarded source table, an engineer wants to quickly understand column-level null rates, distinct value counts, min/max ranges, and value distributions — without writing custom aggregation SQL for every column. What's the fastest way to get this in a Databricks notebook?

options.label: Manually write a GROUP BY/COUNT DISTINCT query per column
Use built-in data profiling (e.g. DataFrame.summary()/describe(), or the profiling tab in the notebook table viewer) to get summary statistics across all columns at once
Export the table to Excel and use PivotTables
There is no built-in profiling capability; a third-party library must be installed

questions.explanation: Databricks notebooks provide built-in profiling: `DataFrame.summary()`/`describe()` compute count, mean, stddev, min/max, and percentiles across all columns in one call, and the notebook's table result viewer includes a Data Profile tab that visualizes null rates and distributions automatically — no per-column custom queries needed.

codeSnippet.code: display(spark.table("prod_sales.bronze.new_source").summary())

questions.prompt: A source CSV file has a `discount_pct` column that arrives as text like "15%" and an `order_id` column that arrives as text but is always numeric. The silver table needs discount_pct usable in arithmetic and order_id efficiently joinable/indexable. What's the correct approach?

options.label: Leave both columns as STRING, since Delta Lake automatically infers correct types at query time
Cast both columns to BOOLEAN, since Delta Lake performs best with the smallest possible data types

Cast order_id to a numeric type (e.g. BIGINT/INT) for efficient joins, and parse/cast discount_pct into a numeric type (e.g. DOUBLE) after stripping the '%' — choosing types deliberately based on how each column will be used
Store discount_pct as STRING and order_id as DOUBLE, since floating point types are always safest for joins

questions.explanation: Choosing appropriate column data types is a deliberate transformation step: numeric IDs used in joins should be numeric types (better performance, correct semantics) rather than strings, and columns needing arithmetic (like a percentage) need to be parsed into numeric types rather than left as text. Type inference alone doesn't fix malformed or oddly-formatted text.

questions.prompt: A bronze orders table has duplicate rows from an at-least-once delivery source, and a `customer_email` column that's sometimes NULL but should default to "unknown@example.com" for downstream joins to work. Which transformation sequence correctly addresses both issues?

options.label: dropDuplicates() with no arguments should be used instead, since column-scoped deduplication is not supported in Spark
coalesce() removes duplicate rows, and dropDuplicates() fills null values
This code silently fails because withColumn cannot be chained after dropDuplicates

dropDuplicates(["order_id"]) removes rows with a repeated order_id (keeping one), and coalesce() fills nulls in customer_email with the default — correctly resolving both the duplicate and missing-value issues

questions.explanation: `dropDuplicates(["order_id"])` deduplicates based on a specific key column (appropriate when only certain columns define uniqueness), and `coalesce()` returns the first non-null argument — a standard pattern for substituting a default value for nulls. Both operations are valid to chain via withColumn.

codeSnippet.code:
from pyspark.sql import functions as F

clean_df = (
    raw_df
    .dropDuplicates(["order_id"])
    .withColumn("customer_email", F.coalesce(F.col("customer_email"), F.lit("unknown@example.com")))
)

questions.prompt: A gold table needs total revenue per region per month, computed from a silver orders table with one row per order. Which transformation is required?

options.label: filter narrows rows to completed orders, groupBy establishes the region/month grouping, and agg(sum) computes the aggregate — the standard filter/group/aggregate pattern
groupBy alone is sufficient; filter and agg have no effect on the result
This requires a join, not a groupBy, since revenue aggregation always needs a second table
date_trunc is invalid inside groupBy and must be computed in a separate step first

questions.explanation: This is the canonical filter → group → aggregate transformation pattern: filtering rows down to what should be counted, grouping by the dimensions of interest (region and month), then aggregating the measure (sum of amount) per group. date_trunc can be used directly as a groupBy expression, and no join is needed since everything comes from one orders table.

codeSnippet.code:
gold_df = (
    orders_df
    .filter(F.col("status") == "completed")
    .groupBy("region", F.date_trunc("month", "order_date").alias("month"))
    .agg(F.sum("amount").alias("total_revenue"))
)

questions.prompt: You need a list of customer_ids that exist in this month's active_customers table but did NOT exist in last month's active_customers table (i.e., newly active customers). Which set operation is the correct fit?

options.label: INTERSECT, which returns rows present in both tables
EXCEPT (also called MINUS in some SQL dialects), which returns rows in the first result set that are not present in the second — exactly "new this month"
UNION, which combines and deduplicates rows from both tables
A LEFT JOIN with no WHERE clause filtering, which returns the same result as EXCEPT by default

questions.explanation: EXCEPT returns rows from the first query that don't appear in the second — precisely the "present now, absent before" semantics needed to find newly active customers. INTERSECT would find customers active in both months; UNION would combine all customers from both months, not isolate the difference.

codeSnippet.code:
SELECT customer_id FROM this_month_active
EXCEPT
SELECT customer_id FROM last_month_active

questions.prompt: A source system exports monthly sales as one row per product with separate columns `jan_sales`, `feb_sales`, ..., `dec_sales`. A downstream dashboard needs one row per (product, month) instead, to plot a time series. Which transformation is needed?

options.label: PIVOT, to turn the month columns into more columns
A UNION of 12 separate SELECT statements is the only way to achieve this
UNPIVOT, which converts wide-format columns (one per month) into a long/tall format with one row per product-month combination — exactly what a time series plot needs
No transformation is needed since dashboards can plot wide-format data natively

questions.explanation: UNPIVOT reshapes wide data (multiple columns representing categories, here months) into long/tall format (one row per category value) — the standard transformation for feeding time-series or category-based visualizations that expect one row per (entity, category). PIVOT does the opposite: long-to-wide.

codeSnippet.code:
SELECT product_id, month, sales
FROM wide_sales
UNPIVOT (
  sales FOR month IN (jan_sales, feb_sales, mar_sales, apr_sales)
)

questions.prompt: A silver customers table needs to be kept in sync with an upstream source: existing customers should have their attributes updated if changed, new customers should be added, and no existing rows should be duplicated. Which load operation directly supports this in one statement?

options.label: INSERT INTO, which appends all source rows regardless of whether they already exist in the target
APPEND, a dedicated SQL keyword for upserts
CREATE OR REPLACE TABLE, which is the only way to merge new and existing data
MERGE, which performs conditional update-if-matched / insert-if-not-matched (an upsert) in a single atomic statement based on the join key

questions.explanation: MERGE INTO is Delta Lake's upsert primitive: it joins source to target on a key and applies different logic per match outcome — UPDATE for matched rows (existing customers with changes), INSERT for unmatched source rows (new customers) — all atomically. Plain INSERT INTO would create duplicates for existing customers rather than updating them.

codeSnippet.code:
MERGE INTO prod_sales.silver.customers AS target
USING staging_customers AS source
ON target.customer_id = source.customer_id
WHEN MATCHED THEN UPDATE SET *
WHEN NOT MATCHED THEN INSERT *

questions.prompt: A silver orders table must never contain a NULL order_id, and order_quantity must always be greater than zero. The team wants these rules enforced at write time so bad data never lands in the table, rather than caught later by a downstream audit query. Which mechanism enforces this?

options.label: Delta Lake CHECK constraints, which reject any write violating the condition, enforcing nullability and range rules directly at write time
A nightly SQL query that reports rows violating the rule, run after the data has already landed
Column comments describing the expected rule, which Spark enforces automatically
There's no way to enforce this in Delta Lake; validation must happen entirely in application code before the write

questions.explanation: Delta Lake supports CHECK constraints (and NOT NULL) that are enforced at write time — any INSERT/UPDATE/MERGE violating the condition is rejected, preventing bad data from ever landing rather than relying on after-the-fact detection. This directly implements nullability and range/cardinality-style validation rules declared on the table itself.

questions.prompt: An upstream source occasionally sends a `signup_date` field as a malformed string (e.g. "N/A" instead of a date) that doesn't match the target column's DATE type. The team wants the pipeline to keep running and route only the bad rows elsewhere for review, rather than crash the whole job or silently coerce bad values into nulls without visibility. What approach fits?
